title: Glasgow's Mister Singh's Hosted Team India, Then a Map on Its Napkins Sparked Outrage
excerpt: Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain called out the iconic Punjabi restaurant after its printed napkins displayed an India map missing the entire Northeast region.
body:
• Mister Singh's India, a 30-year-old Glasgow restaurant, hosted Indian athletes after the Commonwealth Games — but its napkins featured an India map omitting the Northeast
  • Assam boxer and Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain publicly called out the error, saying "every part of India is important"
  • Boxing Federation of India President Ajay Singh noted the map also depicted Jammu & Kashmir incompletely and urged the restaurant to withdraw the merchandise
  • The restaurant, founded by a Punjabi immigrant family in 1994, is famous for its Haggis Pakora and has hosted touring teams and dignitaries for decades

A celebration dinner turned into a diplomatic flashpoint when members of India's Commonwealth Games contingent noticed that napkins at a popular Glasgow Indian restaurant displayed a map of India with the entire Northeast region erased.

The restaurant, Mister Singh's India, hosted Indian athletes after their record-breaking boxing campaign at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games. But Olympic bronze medallist Lovlina Borgohain — herself from Assam, one of the eight Northeastern states — spotted the omission on printed napkins and a display outside the establishment.

"The map on the napkins is missing our North East. Every part of India is important and should be represented," Borgohain told IANS.

Boxing Chief Escalates the Criticism

Boxing Federation of India President Ajay Singh backed Borgohain, pointing out additional inaccuracies including an incomplete depiction of Jammu & Kashmir. Singh urged the restaurant's management to immediately withdraw the faulty merchandise and correct the map to reflect India's complete territorial boundaries.

Mister Singh's India, located at 149 Elderslie Street in Glasgow's Charing Cross area, has not issued an official statement on the matter, according to NDTV. The restaurant is a well-known fixture in the city, frequently visited by touring sports teams and dignitaries from India and across the Commonwealth.

The controversy arrived at an otherwise triumphant moment for Indian boxing. The squad claimed seven gold medals in Glasgow — its highest-ever gold haul at a Commonwealth Games — plus three silvers, including one for Borgohain herself in the women's 75kg category.

Three Decades of Punjabi Heritage in Scotland

Founded in 1994 by Sardar Jit Singh, known as Papa Singh, Mister Singh's India set out to bring the warmth and flavours of Punjab to Glasgow. Four generations of the Singh family now run the restaurant, preserving family recipes and traditional cooking techniques that have earned it a loyal following among locals and visitors over more than three decades.

The restaurant is perhaps best known for its Haggis Pakora — a signature creation that reimagines Scotland's national dish through an Indian lens. Its menu blends curry-house staples like chicken tikka and biryanis with Scottish-Indian innovations, alongside a retail line of family recipe products. TripAdvisor reviewers frequently praise its hospitality, including a tradition of framing photos of diners at their tables.

"The map on the napkins is missing our North East. Every part of India is important and should be represented."

— Lovlina Borgohain, Olympic medallist and CWG 2026 silver medallist

Why the Map Matters to the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the accurate depiction of India's territorial boundaries carries deep political and emotional significance. The Northeastern states — Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, and Sikkim — are home to over 45 million people and have long contended with perceptions of being marginalised within India itself. Seeing them erased on a map at an overseas restaurant celebrating Indian identity struck a raw nerve.

Borgohain, who won bronze at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and gold at the 2023 World Championships, has become one of the most prominent sporting voices from India's Northeast. Her willingness to speak out publicly underscored how the issue extends beyond cartographic accuracy into questions of representation and national identity.

What Happens Next

The restaurant's owners acknowledged the mistake and promised to rectify it, according to NDTV Food. Whether that translates into new merchandise and signage remains to be seen. For now, the incident has drawn fresh global attention to a 30-year-old family restaurant that has long positioned itself as a bridge between Indian and Scottish cultures — and raised questions about how carefully diaspora institutions represent the country they celebrate.
nri_angle: The controversy highlights how diaspora-run restaurants abroad represent India's identity — and the emotional weight of accurate territorial depiction for overseas communities.
